svg.title: Figure 1 | Deep-learning discovery of gut-microbiome antimicrobial peptides differentiating Alzheimer’s disease from healthy controls

g.text: Pore formation in the bacterial membrane

text.tspan: Figure 1 | Deep-learning mining of the gut microbiome identifies antimicrobial peptides that distinguish Alzheimer’s disease from healthy controls.
(a) Discovery workflow: faecal shotgun metagenomes from 62 patients with Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and 64 age- and sex-matched

g.text: healthy controls (HC) were assembled, screened for small open reading frames (smORFs, 30–300 bp), and classified with a bidirectional LSTM plus attention encoder. (b) Principal-coordinate analysis of Bray–Curtis dissimilarity; ellipses denote 95% confidence regions. (c)

Receiver-operating characteristic for held-out candidate AMP classification against two ablations. (d) Candidate AMP load per group; boxes show median and interquartile range, whiskers 1.5× IQR, points individual participants. (e) Volcano plot of differential abundance across

all 2,349 candidate AMPs. (f) Row-scaled abundance of the seven most discriminative peptides with correlated taxa. (g) Enrichment of peptide families in AD, shown as odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals. (h) Schiffer–Edmundson projection and physicochemical properties of

the top candidate. (i) Proposed membrane-disruption mechanism and minimum inhibitory concentrations against a Gram-negative and Gram-positive panel. Statistical tests are named in the corresponding panels; all P values are two-sided and corrected for multiple comparisons by
the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. Values shown are illustrative.
